title: Cache Replacement Policies
summary: LRU and its cheaper approximations — which line gets evicted when a set is full, and why true LRU doesn't scale.

slides.subTitle: Which line has to go?
slides.markdown:
Placement policy (previous topic) decides where a block *could* live; **replacement policy** decides what happens when the set it must go into is already full. Some resident line has to be evicted to make room.

This only matters for set-associative and fully associative caches — direct-mapped caches have no choice to make, since each block has exactly one possible slot and simply overwrites whatever was there.

slides.subTitle: LRU
slides.markdown:
**LRU** evicts whichever line in the set was accessed longest ago, betting that a line untouched for a while is the least likely to be touched again soon — a direct application of temporal locality.

In practice, LRU approximates the theoretical best (Belady's optimal, below) surprisingly well for typical workloads, which is why it's the default goal, even though true LRU is expensive to implement exactly at high associativity.

slides.subTitle: FIFO and Random
slides.markdown:
**FIFO** evicts the line that's been resident longest, regardless of how recently it was used — simple to track (just a queue), but it can evict a line that was just accessed a moment ago if it happened to arrive first.

**Random** picks a victim with no tracking at all — nearly free in hardware, and surprisingly competitive with LRU on some workloads, because it avoids LRU's worst-case pathological access patterns. Both trade some hit rate for much simpler hardware than true LRU.

slides.subTitle: Why hardware cheats
slides.markdown:
Exact LRU needs to track the full recency ordering of every way in a set, which grows combinatorially with associativity — an 8-way set has 8! possible orderings to represent. Real hardware instead uses cheap approximations: **clock** (a reference bit swept round-robin) or **pseudo-LRU** (a small tree of bits that tracks "roughly which half was used more recently" rather than an exact order).

These get within a percent or two of true LRU's hit rate at a small fraction of the tracking-bit cost — the standard engineering trade in every modern cache above a few ways.

slides.subTitle: A 4-way set over time
slides.markdown:
Each access reshuffles the recency order within the set.

![An LRU stack updating across a sequence of accesses in a 4-way set](assets/lru-stack-update.svg)

An access to a way already in the set pulls it to the "most-recent" end; a miss evicts whichever way sits at the "least-recent" end and installs the new line in its place.

assets.alt: An LRU stack updating across a sequence of accesses in a 4-way set

slides.subTitle: A worked trace
slides.markdown:
```text
4-way set, LRU. Accesses: A, B, C, D, A, E

A -> miss, set = [A]              (MRU: A)
B -> miss, set = [A,B]            (MRU: B)
C -> miss, set = [A,B,C]          (MRU: C)
D -> miss, set = [A,B,C,D]  (full) (MRU: D)
A -> hit,  reorder                 (MRU: A, then D,C,B)
E -> miss, set full -> evict B     (least-recently-used)
           set = [A,C,D,E]         (MRU: E)
```

B gets evicted, not C or D, because the hit on A moved A to most-recently-used without touching B, C, or D's relative order — B had been idle the longest.

slides.subTitle: LRU vs Belady's optimal
slides.markdown:
| Policy | Knowledge used | Implementable online? | Typical hit rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Belady's optimal (MIN) | Evicts the line used furthest in the *future* | No — requires knowing the future access sequence | Theoretical best-case |
| LRU | Evicts the line used furthest in the *past* | Yes | Close to optimal for most workloads |

**How to decide:** Belady's MIN is a benchmark, not a real policy — no cache can see the future. It exists purely to measure how close LRU (or FIFO/random/pseudo-LRU) gets to the theoretical ceiling, which is usually within a few percentage points for typical access patterns.
